name: Carla Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a bulldozer at an open-cut coal mine, the same valley my dad worked in for thirty-one years. Most of the day I push overburden, the rock and dirt that sits on top of the coal, off the edge so the diggers can get to the seam. Twelve-hour shifts, four on and four off, and I'm at the gate by quarter to six.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that you can see what you've done at the end of a shift: a clean bench, a straight edge, no mess for the next crew. What wears me out is wet days, when the dozer slides and you're fighting it for twelve hours. And the paperwork they keep adding, honestly, forms for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, and I'd say it at the dinner table first. My fiancé Sam and I have been hearing about robots for years, and the dozer still needs me in it. I don't post online; I don't see the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my worry anyway. My worry is coal: the company keeps talking about the mine running to 2035, and nobody believes the date. AI going flat doesn't change the fact that half the country wants my mine shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep my head down. Sam and I are getting married in April, so every spare cent is going into the wedding and the deposit on the hall. After that I'd get the savings back up from about two months to four, before we think about kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly, but not easy. It's the same feeling I've had since I started: good job, good pay, and a closing date hanging over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Sam work at the mine too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam's a boilermaker in the mine workshop, he welds and fixes the big steel on the machines. So yes, both our pays come out of the same hole in the ground. My mum says that's putting all the eggs in one basket, and she's right, but it's the basket we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad say about all of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad did thirty-one years underground at the old pit and retired with his back in pieces but the house paid off. I'd like that, without the back. I'm not after anything fancy, just to do what he did and do it well.

say: I'd say **I told you so**, first at the dinner table with her fiancé Sam.
She'd point out the **dozer still needs her**, and wouldn't post anything online.
think: AI was never her real worry; the **future of coal** is.
Nobody believes the company's **2035 closing date**, and AI going flat doesn't change that.
do: Keep working her **four-on, four-off** shifts and keep her head down.
Put every spare cent into the **April wedding** and the hall deposit.
Rebuild savings from **two to four months** before thinking about children.
feel: **Settled** but never fully easy, with a closing date always hanging over the job.
S0.quote: AI going flat doesn't change the fact that half the country wants my mine shut.
fieldNote: Her pressure comes from **coal politics**, not technology, and AI Plateau leaves it untouched.
Both she and Sam are paid by **the same mine**, which her mother calls one basket.
Her goal is her father's path: a **paid-off house**, without the ruined back.

steps.text: Keep working four-on, four-off shifts on the dozer
Pay off the April wedding and hall deposit first
Rebuild savings from two months to four after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let them try to get a computer to push dirt in the rain. Office people might need to worry, but a dozer on a wet bench is another thing. At work I'd say the same: we'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the forms might get easier, and I wouldn't miss them. The mine already has GPS on the dozers that shows me the grade on a screen, and I mostly ignore it. If robots come slowly, I reckon I'm fine for a good while, and the coal closing comes first anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much, if I'm honest. I'd do my shifts and keep saving after the wedding. I wouldn't do any course on AI; I've never used one of those chat things and I don't plan to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit wary, the way you are when management says "exciting changes" at a meeting. Usually it means more paperwork and fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office, the planners and the people who order the parts. Jenny in the stores office has been there twenty years and could find a filter for a 1990s grader blindfolded. If a computer does the ordering, I don't know what happens to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try one of the AI tools, even just to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm not against hard work; I'm against being told what to think by my phone. If the boss makes it part of the job, I'll learn the button I have to press, and that's it.

say: She'd challenge anyone to get a computer to **push dirt** in the rain.
At work she'd say office people should worry, and dozer drivers will **wait and see**.
think: The **forms** might get easier, and she already ignores the dozer's GPS screen.
Slow robots mean she's fine **for a good while**, with coal closing first anyway.
do: Keep doing her shifts and **saving after the wedding**.
Refuse any **AI course**, and learn only the button the boss requires.
Wait to see what management's **"exciting changes"** actually mean.
feel: **Wary**, like hearing management announce exciting changes, which usually means fewer people.
S1.quote: I'm not against hard work; I'm against being told what to think by my phone.
fieldNote: She sees the **office staff**, like Jenny in stores, as the people really at risk.
Her refusal of AI is about **independence**, not laziness.
She takes slow robot spread as **breathing room** and makes no new plans.

steps.text: Keep pushing overburden on her usual dozer shifts
Wait to see what management's changes mean before acting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say whoever's letting this happen should be ashamed, the tech companies and the politicians who wave them through. At church I'd say we need to look after each other, because nobody else will. I'd still not post it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly? The office goes in 2028, and by 2031 there's a robot dozer that doesn't slide on wet days. That's me and Sam both, same mine, same few years. Three years is not long when you've just got married and want a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the wedding back to the church and a barbecue at Mum and Dad's, and get the hall deposit back if I can. I'd put the kids on hold. And Sam and I would talk about moving into my parents' back flat for a year or two to bank the rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. It's the feeling you get when the dozer tilts more than it should and you're waiting to see if it settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain, given there are three years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd think about it, but going back to school to sit at a computer isn't me. Maybe a truck licence for the roads, but those will have robots too, won't they? I really don't know what I'd learn that a robot wouldn't do by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be okay this year and maybe next, and after that I don't know. Dad would say his door's open, and Mum would cry and then make a list. I'd be the one not sleeping.

say: She'd blame the **tech companies** and the politicians who wave them through.
At church she'd say people need to **look after each other**, because nobody else will.
think: Office work goes in 2028 and a **robot dozer** arrives around 2031.
She and Sam are paid by the **same mine**, so both jobs go together.
do: Cut the wedding to **church and a barbecue** and try to recover the hall deposit.
Move into her **parents' back flat** for a year or two to bank the rent.
feel: **Sick**, like a dozer tilting too far and waiting to see if it settles.
S2.quote: Three years is not long when you've just got married and want a baby.
fieldNote: The three-year robot gap brings her **no comfort**, because both household incomes go together.
She **resists retraining** and genuinely can't name a skill robots won't take by 2031.
Her safety net is **family**, her parents' back flat, not government help.

steps.text: Cut the wedding to church and a barbecue at her parents'
Put plans for a baby on hold
Move into her parents' back flat to bank the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is more than the government usually gives anyone, so they'd better use it. At work I'd say the young ones should think about it, and the rest of us will do our shifts. I'd be the one saying don't panic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's mostly the same as the fast one, just later. Robots around 2034, and the mine's supposed to close in 2035 anyway, so the two clocks run together. I'd be 35, married, maybe with a little one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding we planned, but no honeymoon overseas, just a week on the coast. I'd push the savings hard, toward six months, and we'd hold off buying a house until we know which way it's going. I'd keep doing my job and see what the company offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a slow worry, not the sick one. Like hearing a storm is coming next week; you check the roof and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd see what the company offers. Would you take a retraining offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if the company paid for it and it was hands-on. Something like fitting or electrical, where you're still on the tools. But I'd want to see someone else go first and come out the other side in a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to see go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would go first; he's more open to that sort of thing than me. He's already a tradesman, so it might be a short step for him to working on the robots. If he does it and it works, I'd follow.

say: She'd say five years is more notice than **government** usually gives anyone.
She'd tell young workers to think ahead, and everyone else **not to panic** yet.
think: Robots around **2034** and the mine's 2035 closing date run together.
She'd be **35**, married, maybe with a baby, when both clocks run out.
do: Have the wedding but swap the overseas honeymoon for a **week on the coast**.
Push savings toward **six months** and hold off on buying a house.
Keep working and wait to see what **retraining** the company offers.
feel: **Worried**, but a slow worry, like a storm forecast for next week.
S3.quote: Robots around 2034, and the mine's supposed to close in 2035 anyway, so the two clocks run together.
fieldNote: She'd consider **hands-on retraining** only if paid for and proven by someone else first.
Her fiancé Sam is the more **open** one, and she'd follow if his move worked.
Robot timing and the **coal closing date** blend into one deadline for her.

steps.text: Swap the overseas honeymoon for a week on the coast
Push household savings toward six months of costs
Hold off buying a house until the picture is clearer
Wait for the company's retraining offer before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and things change; plenty of predictions never happen. At work I'd say my dad was told the pit would close in 1995, and it ran another twenty years. That's what I'd say, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 40 by 2039, and the mine's due to shut before then. So robots aren't really what ends my dozer job in this one, coal is. I've lived with that one my whole working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with everything: the April wedding, the house, probably a baby in a couple of years. I'd keep my shifts and keep saving. Somewhere around 2030 I'd look at what the company's doing and decide then, not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, the same as now really. Ten years is too far off to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is waiting until 2030 leaving it late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But you can't live your whole life getting ready for something that might not come. My grandmother used to say tomorrow has enough worries of its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had children, what would you want for them in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my kids to learn a trade, and to stay near family. Not because of the robots, because that's how you have a good life: work with your hands, go to church, look after your people.

say: She'd say ten years is long and **plenty of predictions** never come true.
She'd mention her dad's pit, told it would close in 1995, **ran twenty years** more.
think: In this picture, **coal closing** ends her dozer job before robots do.
She's lived with that **closing date** for her whole working life.
do: Go ahead with the **April wedding**, the house and probably a baby.
Keep her **dozer shifts** and keep saving.
Look again **around 2030** at what the company is doing before deciding anything.
feel: **Pretty calm**, because ten years feels too far off to lose sleep over.
S4.quote: You can't live your whole life getting ready for something that might not come.
fieldNote: She meets long timelines with **family memory**: her dad's pit outlived its closing date.
She **defers all decisions** to around 2030, a choice she defends with her grandmother's saying.
Her hopes for future children rest on **trade, church and family**, not on technology.

steps.text: Keep working her dozer shifts and saving each month
Go ahead with the April wedding, a house and a baby
Wait until about 2030 to decide on any change

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes me and Sam at once, right when we're starting out. What would help is real jobs, not handouts: apprenticeships that pay a wage while you learn, and companies made to keep some people on. And I'd want my family close, because that's what actually gets you through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of us at the mine go to church, and that's where people would turn first, before any government office. Nobody in the city ever asks what the church hall does for a mining town when things go bad.

headlineQuote: Nobody in the city ever asks what the church hall does for a mining town when things go bad.
portrait: Carla is 27 and drives a **bulldozer** at an open-cut coal mine in the valley where her father worked.
She's marrying **Sam**, a boilermaker at the same mine, in April, so both incomes depend on one site.
She **never uses AI** and resists change, trusting family, church and hard work over technology.
Her steady worry is **coal closing**, and fast AGI turns that into alarm about both jobs at once.
Given more time, she **waits and sees**, deferring decisions and following only proven paths.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it takes her job and Sam's at once, just as they start married life.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** and companies required to keep some workers on, not handouts.
Having her **family close**, which she sees as what really gets people through.
